intro.text: Rule: errors that affect only one side of an account (one-sided errors) disturb the agreement of the trial balance and are rectified through the Suspense Account. intro: Course: Fundamentals of Accounting (B2UBA25207). The questions below are mapped to the nine units of the syllabus and the five course outcomes (CO1–CO5). Five important 5-mark questions are given for each unit, with model answers. Numerical answers have been checked arithmetically.

questions.question: Define accounting. Explain the objectives of accounting. (5 marks) [CO1]

answer.text: The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) defines accounting as the art of recording, classifying and summarising, in a significant manner and in terms of money, transactions and events which are, in part at least, of a financial character, and interpreting the results thereof. Its main objectives are:

rows: Systematic recording: to keep a complete and orderly record of all business transactions so that nothing depends on memory.
Ascertaining profit or loss: to find the result of operations for a period through the Trading and Profit & Loss Account.
Ascertaining financial position: to show assets, liabilities and capital on a given date through the Balance Sheet.
Control over assets and prevention of fraud: proper records help safeguard business property and detect errors and frauds.
Providing information to users: owners, management, creditors, banks, investors and the government rely on accounting information for decisions and statutory compliance.

questions.question: Explain any five accounting concepts. (5 marks) [CO1]

rows: Business Entity Concept: the business is treated as separate from its owner; hence capital is a liability of the business and drawings reduce capital.
Money Measurement Concept: only transactions that can be measured in money are recorded (e.g., employee morale is not recorded).
Going Concern Concept: the business is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future; hence fixed assets are shown at cost less depreciation, not at realisable value.
Dual Aspect Concept: every transaction has two aspects – debit and credit – giving the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

Accrual and Matching Concept: revenues are recognised when earned and expenses when incurred, and expenses of a period are matched against the revenues of that period (basis for outstanding and prepaid adjustments).

questions.question: Explain the accounting conventions. (5 marks) [CO1]

rows: Convention of Consistency: the same accounting methods (e.g., method of depreciation, stock valuation) should be followed year after year so that results are comparable.
Convention of Full Disclosure: all material information must be disclosed in the financial statements and notes (e.g., contingent liabilities).
Convention of Materiality: only items significant enough to influence decisions need separate treatment; trivial items (e.g., a stapler) may be expensed.

Convention of Conservatism (Prudence): anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses; e.g., closing stock is valued at cost or market price, whichever is lower, and provision is made for doubtful debts.
Together these conventions guide the preparation of financial statements where the concepts alone do not give a clear answer.

questions.question: Show the accounting equation for the following transactions of Ravi: (a) Started business with cash 1,00,000; (b) Purchased goods on credit 30,000; (c) Bought furniture for cash 20,000; (d) Sold goods costing 15,000 for 20,000 in cash; (e) Paid creditors 10,000. (5 marks) [CO1]

answer.text: In (d) capital increases by the profit of 5,000 ( 20,000 – 15,000). Final position: Assets 1,25,000 = Liabilities 20,000 + Capital 1,05,000.

questions.question: Explain the steps in the accounting cycle. (5 marks) [CO1]

answer.text: The accounting cycle is the sequence of steps repeated in every accounting period:

rows: Identifying and analysing transactions from source documents (invoices, vouchers, receipts).
Recording in the books of original entry – Journal and subsidiary books (cash book, purchases book, sales book, etc.).
Classifying – posting entries to ledger accounts and balancing them.
Summarising – preparing the Trial Balance to check arithmetical accuracy, followed by adjusting entries.
Preparing final accounts (Trading, Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet), passing closing entries and carrying balances forward by opening entries for the next period.

questions.question: What is book-keeping? Distinguish between book-keeping and accounting. (5 marks) [CO1]

answer.text: Book-keeping is the art of recording business transactions in a systematic manner in the books of account. It is the clerical, recording phase that precedes accounting.

rows: Recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and interpreting.
Secondary stage; begins where book- keeping ends.
To ascertain results and financial position and communicate to users.
Routine and clerical; less skill needed.
Analytical; requires professional knowledge and judgement.

questions.question: Explain the classification of accounts and the golden rules of debit and credit under the English (traditional) approach. (5 marks) [CO1]

rows: Accounts of persons – natural (Ravi), artificial (Bank, Company) and representative (Outstanding Salaries, Prepaid Insurance).
Debit the receiver, credit the giver.
Accounts of assets/property – tangible (Cash, Furniture, Machinery) and intangible (Goodwill, Patents).
Debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
Accounts of expenses, losses, incomes and gains (Rent, Salaries, Commission Received).
Debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.

answer.text: Example: Paid rent 5,000 → Rent A/c (nominal, expense) Dr. To Cash A/c (real, goes out).

questions.question: Explain the rules of debit and credit under the American (modern) approach. (5 marks) [CO1]

answer.text: The modern approach is based on the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital (+ Revenue – Expenses – Drawings). Example: Purchased furniture on credit from Modern Furniture 20,000 → Furniture (asset increases) Dr.; Modern Furniture (liability increases) Cr.

questions.question: Classify the following accounts under the traditional and modern approaches: Cash, Capital, Rent, Ravi (debtor), Furniture, Outstanding Salaries, Bank, Goodwill, Discount Allowed, Prepaid Insurance. (5 marks) [CO1]
What is the double entry system? State its features and advantages. (5 marks) [CO1]

answer.text: Under the double entry system, every transaction affects two accounts in opposite directions with equal amounts – one account is debited and the other credited. It was formalised by Luca Pacioli (1494).

rows: Every transaction has two aspects (dual aspect), so total debits always equal total credits.
It records all three classes of accounts – personal, real and nominal – giving a complete record.
Arithmetical accuracy can be checked by preparing a trial balance.
Profit or loss and the financial position can be ascertained through final accounts.
It helps detect errors and frauds, provides comparable data and is accepted by tax authorities and courts.

questions.question: What is a journal? Explain its features and advantages. (5 marks) [CO1]

answer.text: A journal (from the French ‘jour’, meaning day) is the book of original or prime entry in which transactions are first recorded in chronological order, showing the accounts to be debited and credited with a brief explanation (narration).

rows: Features: transactions are recorded date-wise; each entry shows the debit and credit aspects; every entry carries a narration.
Chronological record: gives a complete day-by-day history of business transactions.
Basis for posting: the ledger is posted from the journal, reducing chances of error.
Narration explains each transaction, which helps later verification and audit.
Reduces errors because both aspects of each transaction are recorded together and checked at the time of entry.

questions.question: Explain the format of a journal and the meaning of a compound journal entry and an opening entry with examples. (5 marks) [CO1]

answer.text: A journal has five columns: Date | Particulars | Ledger Folio (L.F.) | Debit Amount | Credit Amount. The account to be debited is written first with ‘Dr.’, the account to be credited on the next line beginning with ‘To’, followed by the narration.

units.title: Books of Second Entry – Ledger and Trial Balance

questions.question: What is a ledger? Explain its features and utility. (5 marks) [CO1]

answer.text: A ledger is the principal book of account in which all accounts (personal, real and nominal) are maintained and to which entries are transferred (posted) from the journal and subsidiary books. It is called the book of final entry.

rows: It contains a separate account for each person, asset, liability, expense and income, in ‘T’ form with Dr. and Cr. sides.
It classifies transactions account-wise, so the net position of each account is known at a glance.
The balance of each account (debtors, creditors, cash, assets) is readily available.
Ledger balances are the basis for preparing the trial balance and final accounts.
It helps management in control – e.g., amounts receivable from and payable to each party.

questions.question: Distinguish between a journal and a ledger. (5 marks) [CO1]

rows: Narration is written for every entry.
Accounts are balanced periodically; balances used for trial balance.

questions.question: Explain the steps in posting journal entries to the ledger and balancing ledger accounts. (5 marks) [CO1]

rows: Open the account to be debited in the ledger; on its debit side enter the date and ‘To [name of the account credited]’ with the amount.
Open the account to be credited; on its credit side enter the date and ‘By [name of the account debited]’ with the amount.
Write the ledger page number in the L.F. column of the journal and the journal folio (J.F.) in the ledger.
To balance, total both sides; write the difference on the shorter side as ‘By Balance c/d’ (debit balance) or ‘To Balance c/d’ (credit balance) so both totals agree.
Bring down the balance on the opposite side at the start of the next period as ‘To Balance b/d’ or ‘By Balance b/d’. Nominal accounts are closed by transfer to the Trading or P&L Account.

questions.question: What is a trial balance? State its objectives and the errors that are not disclosed by it. (5 marks) [CO1, CO3]

answer.text: A trial balance is a statement of debit and credit balances of all ledger accounts on a particular date, prepared to check the arithmetical accuracy of the books.

rows: Objectives: to verify that total debits equal total credits; to provide a summary of ledger balances; and to serve as the basis for final accounts.
Error of omission: a transaction completely omitted from the books.
Error of principle: e.g., purchase of furniture debited to Purchases Account.
Compensating errors: one error cancels the effect of another.
Error of commission (wrong account, correct side) and errors in the books of original entry (wrong amount in the journal) also remain undisclosed.

questions.question: Prepare a trial balance from the following balances: Capital 50,000; Purchases 45,000; Sales 70,000; Debtors 18,000; Creditors 12,000; Rent 6,000; Salaries 9,000; Furniture 15,000; Cash 21,000; Drawings 4,000; Returns Inward 2,000; Returns Outward 1,500; Discount Received 500; Wages 5,000; Opening Stock 9,000. (5 marks) [CO1]
What are subsidiary books? Name them and explain their advantages. (5 marks) [CO2]

answer.text: Subsidiary books are special journals in which transactions of a similar nature are recorded, instead of recording everything in a single journal. They are: Cash Book, Purchases Book, Sales Book, Purchases Returns (Returns Outward) Book, Sales Returns (Returns Inward) Book, Bills Receivable Book, Bills Payable Book, and Journal Proper (for residual entries such as opening, closing, adjustment and rectification entries).

rows: Division of work: different clerks can maintain different books at the same time.
Saving of time and labour: only totals of each book are posted to the impersonal accounts periodically.
Specialisation and efficiency: staff become experts in particular books.
Easy reference and quick information, e.g., total credit sales or purchases of a month.
Better internal check and easy detection of errors and frauds.

questions.question: Explain the petty cash book under the imprest system. (5 marks) [CO2]

answer.text: A petty cash book records small, recurring payments (postage, stationery, cartage, conveyance, refreshments). Under the imprest system:

rows: The chief cashier estimates the petty expenses for a period and gives a fixed amount (the imprest) to the petty cashier at the beginning.
The petty cashier records each payment in an analytical petty cash book that has separate columns for each type of expense.
At the end of the period the columns are totalled and the book is submitted to the chief cashier with vouchers.
The chief cashier reimburses the exact amount spent, so the petty cashier again starts with the full imprest.
Advantages: control over small payments, fewer entries in the main cash book (only column totals are posted), and easy checking at any time (cash in hand + vouchers = imprest).

questions.question: Prepare an analytical petty cash book (imprest 2,000) for May: May 1 received imprest 2,000; May 3 postage 150; May 6 stationery 220; May 9 cartage 180; May 12 tea for staff 90; May 15 courier 120; May 20 bus fare 60; May 25 stationery 140; May 28 cartage 110. (5 marks) [CO2]

answer.text: Total spent 1,070 is reimbursed on 1 June, restoring the imprest to 2,000.

questions.question: Record the following in the Purchases Book of Fashion House: Apr 2 – bought from Gupta & Co. 20 shirts @ 300 and 10 trousers @ 600, trade discount 10%; Apr 10 – bought from Sharma Textiles 50 sarees @ 400, trade discount 5%; Apr 18 – bought furniture on credit from Modern Furniture 15,000; Apr 25 – bought from Khan Bros. 30 bedsheets @ 250. (5 marks) [CO2]

rows: Total posted to the debit of Purchases A/c

answer.text: Note: Furniture bought on Apr 18 is not entered in the Purchases Book because it is not goods for resale; it is recorded in the Journal Proper (Furniture A/c Dr. To Modern Furniture A/c 15,000).

questions.question: Explain the three-column cash book. What is a contra entry? (5 marks) [CO2]

answer.text: A three-column cash book has Discount, Cash and Bank columns on both sides. The debit side records receipts (cash, cheques deposited, discount allowed) and the credit side records payments (cash, cheques issued, discount received). It serves as both a journal and a ledger for cash and bank.

rows: Cash and bank columns are balanced like ledger accounts; the discount columns are only totalled – discount allowed is posted to the debit and discount received to the credit of the respective accounts.
A contra entry is a transaction that affects both the cash and bank columns, e.g., cash deposited into bank or cash withdrawn from bank for office use.
Contra entries are recorded on both sides of the cash book and marked ‘C’ in the L.F. column; no posting to the ledger is required.
Example: Deposited ₹10,000 into bank → debit side ‘To Cash’ in bank column and credit side ‘By Bank’ in cash column.
Withdrawal of cash from bank for personal use is not a contra entry; it is Drawings (bank column only).

questions.question: Explain the types of errors in accounting with examples. (5 marks) [CO3]

rows: Errors of omission: a transaction is omitted completely (e.g., credit purchase not recorded) or partially (e.g., posted to one account only).
Errors of commission: wrong amount, wrong account or wrong side, wrong totalling or wrong balancing (e.g., ₹500 received from Ram credited to Shyam).
Errors of principle: violation of accounting principles, especially capital vs revenue (e.g., purchase of machinery debited to Purchases A/c).
Compensating errors: two or more errors cancel each other’s effect (e.g., Sales book overcast by ₹100 and Purchases book overcast by ₹100).
Errors are also classified as one-sided (affect one account; affect trial balance) and two-sided (affect two accounts; do not affect trial balance).

questions.question: What is a suspense account? When is it opened and how is it closed? (5 marks) [CO3]

answer.text: A suspense account is a temporary account opened to place the difference in the trial balance when the errors causing the difference cannot be located immediately.

rows: If the debit total of the trial balance is short, the difference is placed on the debit side of the Suspense Account, and vice versa.
It allows final accounts to be prepared on time while the errors are being searched for.
As one-sided errors are found, rectification entries are passed through the Suspense Account.
Two-sided errors are rectified without the Suspense Account because they do not affect the agreement of the trial balance.
When all errors are rectified, the Suspense Account closes automatically with nil balance; any remaining balance is shown in the Balance Sheet (debit as asset, credit as liability) until located.

answer.text: 10,000 debited to Purchases A/c; (b) Credit sale to Ram 2,500 not recorded; (c) Rent 3,000 paid to landlord Mohan debited to his personal account; (d) Repairs 800 debited to Building A/c; (e) 1,200 received from Shyam credited to Sham. (5 marks) [CO3]

(Being amount received from Shyam wrongly credited to Sham)

questions.question: The trial balance showed an excess of debit over credit; the difference was put to a Suspense Account. Rectify the errors and prepare the Suspense Account: (a) Sales Book undercast by 1,000; (b) Purchases Book overcast by 500; (c) Discount allowed 200 not posted to Discount Account; (d) Payment of 750 to Raju debited to his account as 570; (e) Returns inward 400 not posted to Returns Inward Account. (5 marks) [CO3]

answer.text: Suspense Account
The original difference was 720 (debit side of the trial balance in excess), placed on the credit side of the Suspense Account.

questions.question: State the errors which do not affect the agreement of the trial balance, with one example each. (5 marks) [CO3]

rows: Complete omission of a transaction – e.g., credit sale to Ravi of ₹5,000 not recorded at all.
Error of principle – e.g., wages paid for installation of machinery debited to Wages A/c.
Posting to the wrong account but on the correct side – e.g., cash received from Anil credited to Anand.
Wrong amount in the book of original entry – e.g., purchase of ₹2,500 recorded as ₹5,200 in the Purchases Book.
Compensating errors – e.g., Ram’s account debited ₹100 short and Shyam’s account credited ₹100 short.

questions.question: What is a Bank Reconciliation Statement? Explain the need for preparing it. (5 marks) [CO3]

answer.text: A Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) is a statement prepared on a given date to reconcile the bank balance as per the cash book with the balance as per the pass book (bank statement) by listing the causes of difference.

rows: To identify the reasons for the difference between the two balances.
To detect errors and omissions in the cash book or by the bank.
To bring the cash book up to date by recording items such as bank charges, interest and direct deposits.
To prevent and detect frauds and misappropriation in bank transactions.
To know the correct bank balance for the Balance Sheet and for decision-making.

questions.question: Explain the reasons for difference between the cash book balance and the pass book balance. (5 marks) [CO3]

rows: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment – recorded in the cash book but not in the pass book.
Cheques deposited but not yet collected/credited by the bank – recorded in the cash book only.
Bank charges, interest on overdraft, standing-instruction payments (insurance, EMI) debited by the bank but not yet recorded in the cash book.
Interest allowed, dividends collected and direct deposits by customers credited by the bank but not yet recorded in the cash book.
Dishonour of cheques and errors committed either in the cash book or by the bank.

questions.question: Distinguish between a cash book and a pass book. (5 marks) [CO3]

On 31 March the cash book of Ravi showed a debit balance of 25,000. Prepare a BRS: (a) cheques issued 8,000 not presented; (b) cheques deposited 6,500 not credited; (c) bank charges 300 not entered in the cash book; (d) interest 450 credited by bank not entered in the cash book; (e) a customer deposited 2,000 directly into the bank. (5 marks) [CO3]

rows: Add: Cheques issued but not presented
Less: Cheques deposited but not credited

questions.question: On 31 March the pass book of Meena showed an overdraft of 15,000. Prepare a BRS to find the overdraft as per the cash book: (a) cheques issued 4,000 not presented; (b) cheques deposited 7,000 not collected; (c) interest on overdraft 600 debited only in the pass book; (d) insurance premium 1,200 paid by the bank under standing instruction; (e) dividend 900 collected by the bank. (5 marks) [CO3]

rows: Add: Cheques issued but not presented
Less: Cheques deposited but not collected
Less: Insurance premium paid by bank

answer.text: Logic: items that make the pass book overdraft larger (interest, insurance debited by bank; cheques deposited not yet credited) are deducted; items that make it smaller (cheques issued not presented; dividend credited) are added.

units.title: Final Accounts of a Sole Proprietor

questions.question: What is a Trading Account? Explain its objectives and the items shown in it. (5 marks) [CO5]

answer.text: A Trading Account is a nominal account prepared at the end of the year to find the gross profit or gross loss arising from the purchase and sale of goods.

rows: Objective: to ascertain gross profit (excess of net sales and closing stock over opening stock, net purchases and direct expenses).
It helps compute the gross profit ratio and compare trading results of different periods.
Debit side: opening stock, purchases less returns outward, and direct expenses (wages, carriage inwards, freight, fuel and power, factory expenses, import duty).
Credit side: sales less returns inward and closing stock.
The balance (gross profit/loss) is transferred to the Profit & Loss Account.

questions.question: What are adjusting entries? Explain any five with journal entries. (5 marks) [CO5]

answer.text: Adjusting entries are passed at the end of the accounting period to bring the accounts in line with the accrual and matching concepts, so that the final accounts show the true profit and financial position.

rows: To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c

questions.question: Explain closing entries and opening entries with examples. (5 marks) [CO5]

answer.text: Closing entries are passed at the end of the year to close nominal accounts and stock accounts by transferring them to the Trading and P&L Account. Opening entries are passed at the beginning of the next year to bring forward balances of real and personal accounts.

rows: Trading A/c Dr. To Opening Stock, Purchases, Wages, Carriage Inwards (transfer of debit items).
Sales A/c, Returns Outward A/c Dr. To Trading A/c; Closing Stock A/c Dr. To Trading A/c (credit items).
Profit & Loss A/c Dr. To Salaries, Rent, Depreciation etc.; Commission Received, Discount Received A/c Dr. To Profit & Loss A/c.
Profit & Loss A/c Dr. To Capital A/c (net profit transferred); Capital A/c Dr. To Drawings A/c (drawings closed).
Opening entry: Assets A/c Dr. To Liabilities A/c and To Capital A/c (balances of the previous Balance Sheet brought forward).

questions.question: Distinguish between a Profit & Loss Account and a Balance Sheet. (5 marks) [CO5]

rows: Shows net profit or net loss for the period.
Shows the financial position on a given date.
Prepared for a period (‘for the year ended’).
Prepared as on a date (‘as on’).
Nominal accounts – indirect expenses and incomes.
Real and personal accounts – assets, liabilities and capital.

questions.question: Prepare a Trading Account from: Opening Stock 20,000; Purchases 80,000; Returns Outward 2,000; Wages 6,000; Carriage Inwards 1,500; Sales 1,30,000; Returns Inward 3,000; Closing Stock 25,000. (5 marks) [CO5]
Define depreciation. Explain its need and causes. (5 marks) [CO4]

answer.text: Depreciation is the gradual and permanent decrease in the value of a fixed asset due to use, passage of time or obsolescence. It is the allocation of the depreciable cost of an asset over its useful life.

rows: Need: to ascertain the true profit by matching the cost of the asset with revenue it helps earn.
Need: to show the asset at its proper value in the Balance Sheet and to provide funds for replacement; it is also required by law (Companies Act, Income Tax Act).
Cause – wear and tear due to constant use (machinery, vehicles).
Cause – passage of time (lease, patents, copyrights expire) and depletion of wasting assets (mines, quarries).
Cause – obsolescence due to new technology or change in demand, and accidents.

questions.question: Distinguish between the Straight Line Method and the Written Down Value Method of depreciation. (5 marks) [CO4]

rows: Book value at the beginning of each year.
Assets with uniform use, e.g., furniture, leases, patents.
Assets with higher repairs in later years, e.g., plant, machinery, vehicles.
Depreciation constant, repairs increase; total charge rises over time.
Depreciation falls as repairs rise; total charge fairly even.

questions.question: Explain the factors affecting the amount of depreciation. (5 marks) [CO4]

rows: Cost of the asset – purchase price plus all expenses to bring it to working condition (freight, installation).
Estimated useful life – the period over which the asset is expected to be used.
Estimated residual (scrap) value at the end of useful life.
Method of depreciation chosen (SLM, WDV, etc.) and the rate applied.
Legal provisions and the pattern of use of the asset (e.g., extra shifts increase depreciation).

questions.question: A machine was purchased for 1,10,000 and 10,000 was spent on installation. Its estimated life is 5 years and scrap value 20,000. Calculate the annual depreciation and rate under SLM, and show the book value at the end of each of the first three years. (5 marks) [CO4]

answer.text: Annual depreciation = (Cost – Scrap value) ÷ Useful life = ( 1,20,000 – 20,000) ÷ 5 = 20,000. Rate = 20,000 ÷ 1,20,000 × 100 = 16.67% p.a.
